title: Coordinate Distance: |x₁ − x₂| When the Axis Matches
preview: Anchor on horizontal distance with two positive points. Vary one coordinate's sign, then switch to vertical, until the absolute-value pattern locks in.

body.goal: Students compute distance between points that share an x- or y-coordinate by taking the absolute value of the difference of the OTHER coordinates.
body.launch: Sketch a coordinate plane and plot (2, 0) and (5, 0). Ask: 'how far apart are they?' Most students will say 3. Then plot (−2, 0) and (5, 0) — they'll need to wrestle with the sign. The pattern reveals the |x₁ − x₂| rule.

steps.teacherNote: Anchor — both positive, on x-axis. Subtract.
Vary one thing: sign on x. Push: 'how do you handle the negative?' Reveals |5 − (−3)| = 8.
Mixed signs again. Pattern locks in: |1 − (−6)| = 7.
Switch to VERTICAL — same rule on y-coordinates.
Both points share y. Distance is |x₁ − x₂| = 5.
Shared y again, mixed signs on x.
Shared x, both ys positive (but x is negative — push: 'does that matter?').

enrichmentSteps.teacherNote: Diagonal — Pythagorean preview. They might intuit it.

enrichmentSteps.problem: If two points share y and are 7 apart, what's a possible pair?
enrichmentSteps.teacherNote: Reverse: pick the difference, then build.

enrichmentSteps.problem: (a, b) and (a, c) are 5 apart. What's the relationship between b and c?

body.consolidation: Bring the class back. Ask: 'In one sentence — when two points share an x-coordinate, how do you find the distance?' Push for '|y₁ − y₂|.' Same with shared y → '|x₁ − x₂|.' Then ask: 'Why do we need the absolute value bars?' (Order of subtraction doesn't matter — distance is always positive.)
